title: Teacher Engagement with Online Formative Assessment in EFL Writing During the COVID-19 Pandemic: The Case of China
extended_summary:
This paper examines how EFL writing teachers engaged with online formative assessment during the COVID-19 pandemic and what factors shaped that engagement. The authors ask two questions: how teachers engaged with online formative assessment, and which individual, contextual, and technological factors influenced those engagements. The study is motivated by the rapid shift to online teaching during COVID-19 and the limited research on teachers’ perspectives in online formative assessment for writing.

The study is a qualitative case study of three English-as-a-foreign-language writing teachers in three universities in China. Data came from semi-structured interviews, video-recorded lessons, and instructional materials collected during the spring 2020 semester. The paper focuses on how teachers used information and communication technology (ICT) tools such as Tencent Docs, QQ Messenger, Pigai, Moso Teach, Microsoft Word tools, and CCtalk to support feedback, peer assessment, monitoring, and student engagement in writing.

The authors identify three engagement types: disturbing, auxiliary, and integral. One teacher showed low engagement and skepticism toward ICT and online formative assessment; another took an auxiliary stance, using ICT mainly to support and monitor learning; and a third treated online formative assessment as integral to writing assessment and used ICT more intensively to support learner autonomy. Across cases, engagement was shaped by teacher beliefs, digital literacy, prior teaching/learning experience, institutional support, and the affordances and constraints of the technologies. The paper concludes that supporting teachers’ beliefs, digital literacy, and access to responsive tools is important for effective online formative assessment.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study with three participants and no experimental or quasi-experimental design. It is useful for understanding implementation conditions and moderator patterns, but it provides low causal credibility for estimating intervention effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful implementation insights for online formative assessment in EFL writing, but it reports no quantified student outcome gains. Its impact is therefore modest and primarily contextual rather than outcome-based.

interventions.use_case: online formative assessment in EFL writing using ICT platforms such as Pigai for error analysis, feedback, and collecting student drafts; and Tencent Docs/QQ Messenger/Microsoft tools for teacher and peer feedback delivery in fully online classes

EFL writing support tools and platforms used as part of formative assessment, including automated writing evaluation (Pigai), collaborative document tools (Tencent Docs), and messaging platforms for conferencing and feedback

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative case study of three EFL writing teachers (n=3) found that ICT-enabled formative assessment could support writing feedback and peer assessment, but its effectiveness depended heavily on teacher engagement and context. Yuchen and Xiaofang used platforms such as Pigai and Tencent Docs to provide more timely, focused feedback and peer feedback training, whereas Manyun reported that online assessment did not improve students' writing as well as face-to-face assessment.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported writing assessment practices and perceived effects on student writing; videoed lessons and interviews

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that online formative assessment affected student motivation and participation in varied ways across cases. Teachers reported that the absence of face-to-face interaction lowered student participation in online writing activities, though ICT-supported feedback and activities were also used to motivate students and create a more supportive classroom climate.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student participation, motivation, and classroom climate

finding.finding_summary: A central finding was that online formative assessment sometimes supported learner autonomy, but only when teachers actively used ICT to guide self-assessment, peer feedback, and independent revision. Manyun de-emphasized autonomy, Xiaofang used ICT mainly to monitor learning, and Yuchen more strongly fostered independent learning through feedback training and directing students to external resources.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported support for learner autonomy, peer assessment, and self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that online tools made writing assessment more timely, flexible, and efficient by reducing spatial and temporal constraints. For example, Tencent Docs enabled quicker sharing and commenting, and Pigai's error analysis helped teachers identify common language errors and target instruction more efficiently.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of timeliness, flexibility, and efficiency of feedback and assessment workflow

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that implementation conditions strongly shaped teacher engagement: institutional training, collegial support, and university expectations promoted use of online formative assessment, while insufficient support discouraged it. The findings are about contextual moderators of adoption rather than student outcome effects.
finding.measure: Institutional support, teacher training, collegial communication, and contextual/technological influences on implementation
